title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a training-data acquisition practice, not a model inference error. Suno admitted it trained on essentially all music files available on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified specific sources including YouTube, Deezer, and Genius. That training produced a system capable of generating output that closely reproduces sections of specific copyrighted recordings, demonstrated by record labels who used targeted prompts to recreate recognisable versions of named songs. The failure was embedded before deployment, in the data collection stage, meaning no post-deployment content filter would have addressed it at its source.

This is a case of a system deployed without rights clearances for the material used to build it. The labels' ability to prompt the system into reproducing distinctive elements of specific recordings suggests the model retained more than general stylistic patterns from its training data. A German court found in favour of the collecting society GEMA, and a US court denied Suno's motion to dismiss artists' copyright claims. Warner Music settled with Suno and formed a joint venture, and Universal Music settled with Udio. Class action suits from independent artists and further suits from music publishers remain active.

What is not established is whether Suno or Udio acted with deliberate intent to infringe, as that allegation appears in lawsuits and class action filings but has not been adjudicated as a finding of fact in the US proceedings. Settlement agreements between some parties do not constitute admissions of liability. The full scope of what was scraped, and the precise mechanisms by which training data influenced outputs, has not been publicly established through any concluded legal finding.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno, accusing them of illegally copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission. The labels claim both companies scraped massive amounts of music to train their AI models and are now generating songs that directly reproduce sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, and the companies have refused to disclose which music they trained on, claiming instead that their use constitutes fair use.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate versions of famous copyrighted songs by using targeted prompts describing specific decades, genres, and artists. Examples include generating songs resembling Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode," Green Day's "American Idiot," and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The labels submitted a thumb drive of AI-generated music as evidence and provided a lengthy list of thousands of specific copyrighted works from artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, and Madonna that they claim were used to train the models without authorization.
